reasons: Only six of the seven sections are described here.
No tests are visible in the packet.
One failed sentence stops the whole switchboard.

terms.meaning: The chance a player wins the whole match from a given point.
How much one point moves the match-win chance.
Code that checks each sentence against the facts it claims.
A named analyst voice the app uses.
Made-up data labelled as not real.
One checked number with a source and a time.

sections.name: File setup
sections.title: Imports for the switchboard
sections.what: Brings in the tennis, basketball and F1 engine helpers, the Lab and desk data helpers, the rights lookup, the tool and claim types, the verifier and the persona list. Users do not see this directly.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code beyond the imports.
sections.watch_out: Some imports are used only in the part of the file not shown here, so removing one may break the Roster tools.

sections.name: EXAMPLE
sections.title: The labelled example match state
sections.what: Defines a made-up tennis match state with fixed numbers and a label saying it is illustrative: two players who each win 64 percent of serve points, in a deciding set at 5 to 5.
sections.why: The label exists so nobody mistakes the example for real data.
sections.watch_out: The label must stay with the numbers wherever they are shown.

sections.name: switchboardFacts, Voice
sections.title: Facts from the example
sections.what: Calculates how much a point matters in the big state and in the opening state, rounds the results to one decimal in percent, and returns them as two facts marked as model estimates. Also defines the shape each voice takes.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. Keeping the numbers in facts lets the verifier check them.
sections.watch_out: The voices rely on the order of the facts (big first, opening second), so reordering them breaks the sentences.

sections.name: VOICES, Voicing
sections.title: Five persona voices
sections.what: Gives each of the five personas two fixed sentences that fill in the big-point and opening-point numbers, each with its own tone, along with the type of the result.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code beyond the persona design: each persona has a distinct voice.
sections.watch_out: Sentences use only those two numbers, so any new wording must keep them or the verifier will reject it.

sections.name: switchboard
sections.title: Builds and checks all voicings
sections.what: Produces each persona's two sentences from the facts, checks every sentence with the verifier, and returns the label, facts and voicings. If any sentence fails, it throws an error naming the persona and the reasons.
sections.why: The comment says a failing template is a bug.
sections.watch_out: Throwing means the whole switchboard fails to load, not just one persona.

sections.name: pp
sections.title: Formats numbers as percentage points
sections.what: Turns a number from 0 to 1 into a percentage with one decimal and the word pts. Also sets a fixed illustrative pit-lane loss of 22 seconds for an F1 tool.
sections.why: The comment says the pit-lane figure is a typical value, not measured for a race.
sections.watch_out: The pit-lane figure is not measured for any race and must not be quoted as real.

sections.name: personaTool
sections.title: Builds each persona's signature tool card
sections.what: Builds the card shown for each persona. The Opener gets live links into the Decision Lab at real IPL chase moments. The Iceman and Closer show example numbers labelled as illustrative. The Architect shows an xG demo from open football data. Any other persona, including the Professor, gets the F1 pit-window demo. If the needed data is missing, the card says it is pending.
sections.why: Likely reason: each persona needs different content, so one function picks what to build. The illustrative and open-data labels tell users which numbers are real.
sections.watch_out: Any persona slug not handled above silently gets the F1 pit-window demo, and the packet cuts off the attribution lines at the end of the Architect and pit-window branches, so those could not be checked.

summary: Builds the Persona Switchboard: the same verified facts from a labelled tennis example, rewritten in five analyst voices, each sentence checked by the claim verifier. The file also contains the tool setup for the Roster, which is not visible in the notes.
purpose: Shows how one set of facts can be voiced differently without changing the numbers.
why: The header says the same verified facts are re-voiced by each analyst with deterministic templates.
how: 1. Computes the point importance for a labelled example state and makes two facts. 2. Gives each persona two fixed sentences that use those numbers. 3. Checks each sentence with the verifier, and throws an error if one fails. 4. Returns the example label, the facts and the voicings. 5. Formats numbers as percentage points. 6. Sets a fixed pit-lane loss figure for an F1 tool.
inputs: No user input. Uses a fixed example and the persona list.
outputs: Facts, two sentences for each persona, the example label, and tool data for the Roster.
risks: The example is illustrative, not a real match, and is labelled as such. A failed verification throws, which would break the switchboard for everyone. The pit-loss figure is typical, not measured.
debug: If the switchboard page errors, look for a verification message naming a persona. Check that each voice's numbers match the two facts in order.
